“Swiss German”, the default, follows the physical keyboard of the same name: ü, ö and ä on the right, é and ë next to the space bar. “Luxembourg” has slightly wider keys, ten per row instead of eleven: é on the right, ä and ë next to the space bar, ü and ö on long press.

This keyboard was designed to preserve and promote Lëtzebuergesch. It gives everyone a modern tool to write the country's language every day:

💡 Word suggestions in Lëtzebuergesch
🔡 The diacritics ë, ä and é right on the keyboard
🇱🇺 A design in the colours of Luxembourg
This keyboard grows by word of mouth. Share it with your family and friends: every share helps Luxembourgish exist a little more on phones.

Word suggestions are built on two open corpora of contemporary Luxembourgish:

📰 LuxAlign: sentences from RTL.lu articles, collected by Fred Philippy et al. (COLING 2025). CC BY-NC 4.0 licence.

📖 LETZ: example sentences from the Lëtzebuerger Online Dictionnaire (lod.lu), collected by Fred Philippy et al. (SIGUL 2024). CC BY 4.0 licence.

The first provides the vocabulary and how words follow each other, the second everyday language.

🇱🇺 Lëtzebuerger Online Dictionnaire (lod.lu), Zenter fir d'Lëtzebuerger Sprooch. CC0 1.0 licence. It provides the translations of the words into English, French, German and Portuguese, and 85,000 forms the press never writes.

🇱🇺 Translation corpus of the Zenter fir d'Lëtzebuerger Sprooch (data.public.lu). CC0 1.0 licence. It provides the English, French and German translations of the example sentences, made by professional translators.

🇫🇷 Lexique 3.83: a French lexical database by Boris New and Christophe Pallier (lexique.org). CC BY-SA 4.0 licence. It provides the 125,000 forms of the second suggestion row, and keeps the spell checker from underlining correct French.

🔤 The words on the collection cards are set in Lora, Cormorant Garamond and EB Garamond, three free typefaces under the SIL Open Font License 1.1.

Let's keep Lëtzebuergesch alive for future generations!

Zero personal data collected: what you type stays on your phone. Only voice typing, when you tap the microphone, sends your voice to the University of Luxembourg, which writes it down without keeping it.
Type “moien” and tap a suggestion: nothing to install to try it
less than a minute after opening
Came back without turning it on
These timestamps stay on your phone.
The keyboard must be turned on and then selected before you can use it, like any third-party keyboard on Android. These interactive steps are also in the “Haut” tab; here is what they look like.

From the Haut tab, the “Open settings” button takes you straight to the Android “On-screen keyboard” screen, where “Lëtzebuergesch Clavier” appears next to your other installed keyboards, with its switch off.
System screen listing the keyboards, switch to turn on

When you turn on the switch, Android shows a generic warning displayed for every third-party keyboard, followed by a second note about restarting the phone. Lëtzebuergesch Clavier collects nothing you type: tap OK on both to continue, then return to the app with the back button.
System warning shown for any third-party keyboard
Back in the app, step 1 is ticked automatically and step 2 unlocks. The “Open the picker” button opens the list of active keyboards: tap “Lëtzebuergesch Clavier” to make it the keyboard in use.

Once both steps are ticked, the Luxembourgish keyboard appears wherever you type, including the test field in the Haut tab. A long press on the space bar lets you switch to another keyboard at any time.
All three steps ticked, keyboard active in the test field
The keyboard starts in letter mode. The first letter of each message is capitalised automatically, as on any standard keyboard.

The letters of Luxembourgish have their own keys: é, ë and ä, plus ü and ö with the “Swiss German” layout (Keyboard settings → Layout). For other accents (è, ê, à, ç...), long press the letter, slide your finger to the accent you want, then let go.
Accent popup on the letter e

A suggestion bar appears above the keyboard as soon as you type. Luxembourgish words come first; French takes over from the third letter if no Luxembourgish word matches. Tap a suggested word to complete it instantly, space included.

Turn on the Luxembourgish spell checker in the system settings (Haut tab, “Keyboard installed”) so your Luxembourgish and French words are no longer underlined in red in Messages, Notes and other apps.
The “123” button at the bottom left of the keyboard switches to numbers and common symbols. Basic punctuation (comma, full stop, apostrophe) stays available directly on the letter keyboard.

Seven games, gathered in the Spiller tab, help you practise Luxembourgish while having fun:

• 🎲 Wuertsich: find the words hidden in a grid.
• 🔤 Wuertmix: put the letters of a word back in order.
• 🟩 Wuertriet: guess a 5-letter word in 6 tries.
• 📝 Wuertlück: complete a real sentence that is missing a word.
• 🔢 Zuelwuert: write out the result of a multiplication in words.
• 🧩 Kräizwuert: a crossword, with clues in English.
• 🔡 Wuertplaz: fit the listed words into an empty grid, with no clues at all.

Every word you win goes into your collection, and the 📚 Leitner box has you review it at longer and longer intervals, until it is learnt.

Every word won in a game becomes a card, kept in “Mäi Carnet” (Spiller tab). Tap a card to open it full size; tap beside it, or flick it up or down, to close it.\n\nThe images below go through the “Waasser” (water) card part by part: each number points to the explanation after the image.

1. The word, as you met it in the game, with its capital if it is a noun.

2. The round badge: the number of letters in the word. “Waasser” has 7.

3. The illustration: its colour shows the field of meaning (life and body, territory, economy, time and measure…), and its pattern is drawn from the letters of the word, so the same word always gives the same picture. A few cards, like this one, also carry a drawing.

4. The frame: its metal tells the rarity of the word. Pewter for Common, bronze for Uncommon, silver for Rare, gold for Very rare. Rarity comes from how often the word is used in Luxembourgish: the 3,000 most common words are common, those beyond number 9,000 very rare. For Zuelwuert numbers, what counts is how hard they are to spell.

5. The word-class line: what the word is according to the official ZLS dictionary (“Neuter noun”, “Verb”, “Adjective”…), then the game where you won it.

6. The meaning, in bold: the English translation of the word.

7. The sentence in italics: an example of the word in use, taken from the official dictionary. For a number, it is how the number is built.

8. The smaller line: the English translation of that sentence, only when the ZLS has published one. Otherwise, the card shows “Same family:” and the other forms of the word (plural, conjugations…).

9. The SEEN shield: how many times you have won this word, across all games.

10. The medallion: the game that gave you the card, recognisable by its emblem and colour, and named around the edge.

11. The LEVEL shield: the Leitner box compartment the card is in, from 1 to 6. It goes up with each successful review, and turns into ✓ when the word is learnt.

12. The serial line: the card's number in your collection and the date you won it.

13. The rank: the word's place among the most frequent words of the language (“#856” for “Waasser”), or “not in corpus” if it does not appear there.
The small card, in the collection grid

The small card keeps only what you need to choose which one to open:

A. The word.

B. The emoji of the game or games where you won it, then the start of its meaning.

C. Six bars, one per Leitner box compartment: they fill up as the card progresses. Here, “Waasser” has passed one.

Every word you type moves your mastery of Lëtzebuergesch forward, shown in the “Mäi Lëtzebuergesch” tab. Eight levels mark the way: 🌍 Ufänker, 🌱 Klengen, 🔥 Fléisseg, 💎 Geschéit, 🦊 Renert, 🦁 Roude Léiw, 👑 Sproochenkënner and 🧙 Sproochenmeeschter.

The Luxembourgish keyboard doesn't appear when I type?
→ Check that it is selected (not just turned on): Haut tab, “Keyboard installed”, step 2, or tap the keyboard icon in the navigation bar at the bottom of the screen while you type.

How do I switch to another keyboard for a moment?
→ Long press the space bar of the Luxembourgish keyboard, then choose another keyboard in the list. To come back to Luxembourgish, use the keyboard icon in the navigation bar: on other keyboards, a long press on the space bar only changes their own language.

Is my data sent anywhere?
→ No: the keyboard works entirely on your device.
In “Languages & input”, open “Spell checker” and choose “Lëtzebuergesch spell checker”

Guess the %1$s-letter Luxembourgish word in at most %2$s tries.

After each try, the colour of the letters tells you:
🟩 Green: right letter, right place
🟨 Orange: the letter is in the word, but in the wrong place
⬜ Grey: the letter is not in the word

Your guess must be a word in the Luxembourgish dictionary.

Every sentence is a real Luxembourgish sentence with one word missing. Of the four options, only one is what the author wrote: the other three are words the corpus attests in the same position, so they sound right as long as you don\'t read the whole sentence.\n\nThe difficulty depends on how common the missing word is: frequent in “Easy”, rare in “Hard”.
The Wuertlück sentences could not be loaded.

A multiplication, and four ways to write its result: only one is correct Luxembourgish. The others are the mistakes people really make: German, swapped digits, the hyphen, the Eifel rule, the -ig ending. When you get it wrong, the game tells you which.

Two rules are enough to write every number up to a hundred. The units come before the tens: 56 is six-and-fifty, “sechsafofzeg”. And the n of the linking word “an” drops before f, s, v, m…, but stays before d, t, z, n, h and vowels. That is the Eifel rule, hence “sechsafofzeg” (56) but “sechsandrësseg” (36).

In “Hard”, the product is no longer shown: you have to work it out before writing it.
Spellings checked against the Lëtzebuerger Online Dictionnaire (LOD), Zenter fir d\'Lëtzebuerger Sprooch, data.public.lu, CC0.
Work it out, then choose the spelling.

Each clue is the English meaning of a Luxembourgish word: write it in the grid, letter by letter, accents included. The keypad follows the layout of the Luxembourgish keyboard, and Ä, Ë, É, Ö and Ü are right there, no long press needed.

Tap a square to choose a word, tap it again to switch direction. A mistake only shows once the word is completely written.

The grid is in capitals, like every crossword. Each word you find reminds you of its real spelling: in Luxembourgish, nouns keep their capital.

The difficulty depends on how rare the words are, not on the size of the grid.

All the words are given: your job is to find where they go. Tap a word in the list, then a square in the grid: the places where it can go light up. Tap a word already placed to take it back.

A word that would contradict a letter already written can't be placed: this is the pencil, not a correction.

Once all the crossings of a word are filled, it locks and gives you its meaning in English. That's the reward, which is why it only comes at that moment. A won word turns green and can't be taken back; its meaning stays readable under the word list.

No knowledge of Luxembourgish is needed to play: the deduction is about lengths and crossings. The difficulty follows the size of the grid and how many words share the same length.

Eight ways to practise your Luxembourgish. The Leitner box gives you access to the cards you\'ve studied. The vocabulary games give you the translation of the words, at a moment when it doesn\'t give the answer away; Zuelwuert is about spelling numbers, Kräizwuert is the only one where you write the words yourself, and Wuertplaz the only one you can play without knowing the language. They all feed the same collection.

To write what you say, the keyboard sends your voice to the LuxASR service of the University of Luxembourg, during voice typing only.

The University turns it into text without keeping it, and without using it to train its models. Like any website, it records the time and IP address of the connection.

What you type never leaves your phone.

Learn more: https://famibelle.github.io/LuxKeyb/privacy/privacy-policy.html#dictee-vocale
